title: The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development: An Empirical Investigation
author: Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson, James A. Robinson
summary:
Synopsis
The paper argues that differences in institutions established during colonialism—specifically, whether colonisers created extractive institutions for resource exploitation or inclusive institutions for settlement—are the primary determinant of long-run differences in economic development across countries. Using settler mortality rates as an instrumental variable, the authors demonstrate that colonies with high mortality rates developed extractive institutions and remain poor today.

title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
author: F A Hayek
summary: Hayek argues that centrally planned economies cannot efficiently allocate resources because no single authority can possess all the dispersed knowledge held by individuals throughout society. He contends that prices in free markets serve as a communication mechanism that efficiently transmits this knowledge, allowing decentralized decision-making to produce superior outcomes compared to top-down economic planning.

title: The Nature of the Firm
author: R. H. Coase
summary: Coase explains why firms exist by arguing that the transaction costs of coordinating economic activity through market mechanisms make internal organization more efficient in certain contexts. He defines the firm as an alternative to the market where an entrepreneur replaces price signals with direct coordination to reduce the costs of negotiating and enforcing contracts.

title: The Road to Serfdom
author: F A Hayek
summary: Hayek argues that central economic planning and government control, regardless of good intentions, inevitably lead to totalitarianism and the loss of individual freedom. He contends that free markets and the rule of law are essential safeguards against the concentration of power that destroys liberty.

title: Deep Learning for Solving Economic Models
author: Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
summary: Jesús Fernández-Villaverde emphasises that deep learning is revolutionising quantitative economics by enabling the solution of dynamic models traditionally hindered by the curse of dimensionality. Neural networks efficiently approximate equilibrium conditions, offering scalable global solutions. Applied to the neoclassical growth model, this approach expands the methodological frontier of computational economic analysis.

title: Housing and Inequality
author: Yannis M. Ioannides, L. Rachel Ngai
summary: Yannis M. Ioannides and L. Rachel Ngai examine housing as both a driver and a reflection of inequality. They highlight three dimensions—consumption, capital, and location—showing how unequal endowments shape housing outcomes and how neighbourhood “memberships” propagate disparities. Their analysis emphasises racial discrimination, segregation, and the role of housing in reinforcing wealth and opportunity gaps.
